analysis.background: Hantavirus pulmonary syndrome (HPS) carries a case fatality rate of 35%‑40% and has no approved pharmacologic treatment (A1).
analysis.methods: The article is a commentary; no study design, sample, or data collection methods are reported (not reported in the supplied evidence).
analysis.results: No clinical data support therapeutic plasma exchange (TPE) in HPS; efficacy remains unproven (A7).
analysis.contribution: The authors provide a mechanistic, hypothesis‑generating rationale that maps HPS immunopathology to TPE targets, emphasize early‑phase timing and plasma‑based replacement, and urge systematic multicenter outcome reporting (A4, A7).
analysis.limitations: Arguments are speculative, lack empirical evidence, and are based on analogy to other diseases; conclusions about benefit cannot be drawn without clinical studies (A7, A5).

analysis.summary_en: Background: HPS has a 35%‑40% case fatality rate and no approved drug treatment. Methods: This is a commentary; no study design or data are reported. Results: No clinical evidence exists that therapeutic plasma exchange improves HPS outcomes. Contribution: The paper offers a mechanistic, hypothesis‑generating rationale linking HPS plasma‑borne mediators to TPE, suggests early‑phase intervention and plasma‑based replacement, and calls for systematic multicenter reporting. Limitations: The proposal is purely speculative, lacks empirical data, and cannot support efficacy conclusions.

papers.title: Detection of new world hantaviruses by a broadly reactive rRT-PCR assay.
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND AND OBJECTIVES: Orthohantaviruses are negative-sense RNA viruses that persistently infect rodents and can cause severe human disease. Orthohantavirus diversity complicates comprehensive surveillance strategies and diagnostic tools. Currently, serological assays and nested PCR with degenerate primers are used for hantavirus diagnosis and rodent surveillance, but these assays have long turnaround-times. Here, a broadly reactive Orthohantavirus real-time PCR assay is presented that can be incorporated into public health and research laboratories across the Americas. STUDY DESIGN: Starting from an existing rRT-PCR primer-probe set originally developed for the detection of Sin Nombre virus, a pan-America Orthohantavirus assay (HantAmeriQ) was developed that can be used for both human and rodent surveillance. RESULTS: Using synthetic RNA, the HantAmeriQ assay detected all New World Orthohantaviruses known to cause human disease at a limit of detection between 25 (Blue River virus) and 28,000 (Bayou virus) copies/reaction. Genetically diverse hantaviruses from North America (including Sin Nombre, New York, Monongahela, Blue River, and Bayou viruses) and Central/South America (including Catacamas, Carrizal, Choclo, Maciel, and Andes viruses) were detected within similar limits. The HantAmeriQ assay performed as well as or better than a commercially available assay for the detection of North American, but not South American hantaviruses and detected diverse hantaviruses from rodent and human specimens. CONCLUSIONS: Here, the HantAmeriQ assay detected New World Orthohantaviruses in both rodent and human samples from across the United States, and hantaviruses from Central and South America. The assay demonstrates strong potential for diagnostic use in North American clinical laboratories and for surveillance and research applications in rodent-centered field studies.

papers.title_zh: 使用广谱 rRT-PCR 检测新世界 汉坦病毒 病毒。

analysis_zh.background: 正汉坦病毒es 是负义链 RNA 病毒,能够持续感染啮齿动物并可导致严重的人类疾病,其遗传多样性使监测和诊断策略复杂化。
analysis_zh.methods: 从最初为 Sin Nombre 病毒设计的 rRT‐PCR 引物‐探针组合中开发出一种泛美洲 正汉坦病毒 实时 PCR 检测(HantAmeriQ),旨在用于人类和啮齿动物的监测。
analysis_zh.results: 使用合成 RNA,HantAmeriQ 检测到所有已知导致人类疾病的新世界 正汉坦病毒es,检测下限在每反应 25 份(Blue River 病毒)至 28,000 份(Bayou 病毒)之间;它同样在相似的检测限内检测到来自北、美洲、中美洲和南美洲的遗传多样的 汉坦病毒es,且其表现不逊于或优于用于北美 汉坦病毒es 的商业检测试剂。
analysis_zh.contribution: 该检测在北美临床实验室的诊断应用以及美洲范围内以啮齿动物为中心的现场监测和研究中具有很大潜力,已在来自美国及中南美洲的啮齿动物和人类样本中检测到 汉坦病毒es。

papers.title: Artificial intelligence for chest imaging in hantavirus pulmonary syndrome: A review of practical considerations for rare-disease imaging.
papers.abstract: Hantavirus pulmonary syndrome (HPS) is an uncommon zoonotic respiratory illness with a high case fatality rate. Recent travel-associated Andes orthohantavirus clusters have renewed interest in early radiographic recognition of the disease outside its usual geographic range. Artificial intelligence (AI) tools developed during the COVID-19 pandemic now inform several radiology workflows, but the application of AI to HPS chest imaging remains largely unexplored. This narrative review summarises the imaging features of HPS across modalities, considers lessons from AI applications in COVID-19 and viral pneumonia imaging, and discusses practical development considerations for HPS-aware imaging AI, including dataset development, label standardisation, realistic comparator inclusion, candidate modelling approaches, external validation, and clinical workflow integration. The review also considers challenges to HPS-aware imaging AI, including data scarcity, low pretest probability in non-endemic settings, overlapping imaging findings, and translational pitfalls from recent AI literature. As HPS is unlikely to support conventional disease-specific model development without coordinated data collection, future work will likely require multi-institutional datasets, prevalence-aware evaluation, and multimodal workflow integration that combines imaging with clinical, laboratory, and epidemiologic context.

papers.title_zh: 人工智能在 汉坦病毒肺综合征 胸部影像中的应用:罕见疾病影像的实用考虑综述。

analysis_zh.background: 汉坦病毒肺综合征是一种罕见的动物源性呼吸系统疾病,致死率高,近期与旅行相关的安第斯病毒 正汉坦病毒 簇再次引起了对在非流行地区早期影像学识别的关注。
analysis_zh.main_directions: 本综述概述了各成像模态的影像特征,提炼了 AI 在 COVID‐19 与病毒性肺炎中的经验教训,并阐明了面向汉坦病毒肺综合征的 AI 实际开发步骤,包括数据集构建、标签标准化、纳入真实对照、建模方法、外部验证以及工作流集成。
analysis_zh.current_state: 在 COVID‐19 大流行期间开发的 AI 工具已用于众多放射学工作流,但 AI 在汉坦病毒肺综合征胸部影像中的应用仍基本未被探索。
analysis_zh.gaps: 主要挑战包括数据稀缺、非流行地区先验概率低、与其他病毒性肺炎的影像表现重叠,以及近期 AI 文献中强调的转化陷阱。
analysis_zh.future_research: 未来工作可能需要协调多机构数据集、考虑患病率的评估,以及将影像与临床、实验室和流行病学信息相结合的多模态工作流集成。

papers.title: Use of tocilizumab for severe hantavirus pulmonary syndrome: a MEURI case series with contextual comparisons.
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND: Hantavirus pulmonary syndrome is a rare zoonotic disease associated with high mortality, acute respiratory failure, shock, capillary leak, and systemic inflammation. Currently, no specific antiviral or immunomodulatory therapy has proven effective for routine clinical use. The current cruise-associated hantavirus outbreak motivated this early descriptive report from an ongoing, larger, pre-post study (ISRCTN72088243). We aimed to describe tocilizumab use under the Monitored Emergency Use of Unregistered and Investigational Interventions (MEURI) framework. METHODS: In this descriptive case series at Hospital Zonal de Bariloche Dr Ramón Carrillo, San Carlos de Bariloche, Argentina, patients with laboratory-confirmed severe hantavirus pulmonary syndrome and requiring intensive care unit (ICU) admission or assessment were eligible to receive tocilizumab in addition to standard supportive care, in accordance with the MEURI framework. Tocilizumab was administered to patients within 24 h of ICU admission or ICU-level evaluation as a single intravenous dose of 8 mg/kg, up to a maximum of 800 mg. During this time, five eligible patients could not receive tocilizumab because timely administration was not feasible due to drug unavailability or refractory shock at diagnosis. This case series represents the first report from the larger, ongoing, pre-post study (ISRCTN72088243). The main descriptive outcome was survival to ICU discharge in patients who received tocilizumab and patients who were eligible to receive tocilizumab but did not. FINDINGS: Between June 1, 2024, and May 5, 2026, 13 patients with laboratory-confirmed hantavirus pulmonary syndrome were evaluated for inclusion after institutional approval of the MEURI protocol. Ten met eligibility criteria for tocilizumab; five received tocilizumab and five did not. In the five eligible non-treated patients, two were diagnosed when they were already in refractory shock, precluding timely administration, and three did not receive tocilizumab because the drug was unavailable when treatment was being considered. Four of five tocilizumab-treated patients survived to ICU discharge. The fifth treated patient died after rapid progression to refractory shock. All five eligible non-treated patients died after ICU admission. INTERPRETATION: These observations suggest that IL-6 inhibition warrants further evaluation within the MEURI framework or analogous expanded-access frameworks, and, when feasible, collaborative randomised studies with standardised data collection. FUNDING: None. TRANSLATIONS: For the Spanish translations of the abstract see Supplementary Materials section.

analysis.background: Hantavirus pulmonary syndrome is a rare zoonotic disease with high mortality, acute respiratory failure, shock, capillary leak, and systemic inflammation (A1). No specific antiviral or immunomodulatory therapy has proven effective for routine use (A2).
analysis.methods: A descriptive case series was conducted under the MEURI framework at Hospital Zonal de Bariloche, Argentina, enrolling laboratory‑confirmed severe HPS patients requiring ICU care (A5). Tocilizumab was given as a single IV dose of 8 mg/kg (max 800 mg) within 24 h of ICU admission (A6). The primary descriptive outcome was survival to ICU discharge comparing treated and eligible non‑treated patients (A9).
analysis.results: Between 1 June 2024 and 5 May 2026, 13 patients were evaluated; 10 met eligibility, five received tocilizumab and five did not (A10‑A13). Four of five treated patients survived to ICU discharge, one died, and all five non‑treated patients died (A14‑A16).
analysis.contribution: The authors interpret that IL‑6 inhibition warrants further evaluation within MEURI or similar expanded‑access frameworks and collaborative randomized studies (A17).
analysis.limitations: Only the abstract is available, providing a small, non‑randomized case series without statistical comparison; thus conclusions are limited (abstract_only).

analysis.summary_en: Background: Hantavirus pulmonary syndrome is a rare, high‑mortality zoonosis with no proven specific therapy (A1, A2). Methods: A descriptive MEURI case series at an Argentine ICU gave tocilizumab 8 mg/kg IV within 24 h to eligible severe HPS patients, assessing survival to ICU discharge (A5‑A9). Results: Of 13 evaluated patients, 5 received tocilizumab (4 survived, 1 died) and 5 eligible non‑treated patients all died (A10‑A16). Contribution: Authors suggest IL‑6 blockade merits further study in expanded‑access or randomized trials (A17). Limitations: Abstract‑only report, small non‑randomized sample limits inference (abstract_only).

papers.title_zh: 托珠单抗用于重症汉坦病毒肺综合征的研究:MEURI病例系列及情境比较。

analysis_zh.background: 汉坦病毒肺综合征 是一种罕见的动物源性疾病,死亡率高,表现为急性呼吸衰竭、休克、毛细血管渗漏和全身炎症 (A1)。目前尚无特异性抗病毒或免疫调节治疗被证实可常规使用 (A2)。
analysis_zh.methods: 在阿根廷巴里洛切地区医院(Hospital Zonal de Bariloche)依据MEURI框架开展描述性病例系列研究,纳入实验室确诊的重症汉坦病毒肺综合征患者,需接受ICU治疗(A5)。在ICU入院后24 小时内(A6),给予托珠单抗单次静脉注射8 mg/kg(最高800 mg)。主要描述性结局为比较接受治疗的患者与符合条件但未治疗患者的ICU出院存活率(A9)。
analysis_zh.results: 2024年6月1日至2026年5月5日期间,共评估13例患者;其中10例符合入选标准,5例接受托珠单抗治疗,5例未接受治疗(A10‐A13)。接受治疗的5例中有4例存活至ICU出院,1例死亡;未治疗的5例全部死亡(A14‐A16)。
analysis_zh.contribution: 作者认为IL‐6抑制值得在MEURI或类似的扩展使用框架以及合作随机研究中进一步评估(A17)。
analysis_zh.limitations: 仅有摘要可得,提供了小规模、非随机的病例系列,缺乏统计学比较;因此结论受限(abstract_only)。

papers.title: Hantavirus risk and preparedness in Europe in an era of climate change and global mobility.
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND: Hantaviruses are rodent-borne zoonoses causing haemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome and hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome. In Europe, Puumala virus (PUUV) and Dobrava virus (DOBV) account for most recognized disease; Seoul virus (SEOV) is relevant to ports and urban settings. The 2026 MV Hondius cruise-ship cluster of Andes hantavirus (ANDV) infections, involving passengers from 23 countries, has highlighted urgent gaps in European preparedness for both endemic and imported hantavirus disease. OBJECTIVES: To review hantavirus epidemiology, ecology, clinical recognition, diagnostics, and preparedness in Europe, with emphasis on endemic PUUV, DOBV, and SEOV, and to clarify the separate relevance of imported ANDV infection for travel medicine and maritime response. SOURCES: We conducted a structured narrative review of literature published from January 2000 to May 2026, prioritizing surveillance reports, systematic and narrative reviews, rodent ecology studies, diagnostic evaluations, external quality assessment studies, and outbreak investigations. WHO, European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control, and International Health Regulations guidance documents were also reviewed. CONTENT: European hantavirus epidemiology is heterogeneous and shaped by reservoir ecology, biome-specific rodent dynamics, clinical awareness, diagnostic capacity, and surveillance practice. Climate effects are indirect and regionally variable, mediated by mast years, predator-prey dynamics, winter conditions, land use, reservoir density, and human exposure. Diagnostic preparedness is uneven, particularly for molecular detection. Imported ANDV infection is rare in Europe but relevant to travel medicine and high-consequence preparedness because it can cause severe hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome and, unlike endemic European hantaviruses, has documented person-to-person transmission. IMPLICATIONS: European preparedness should prioritize PUUV, DOBV, and SEOV through rodent biomonitoring, harmonized surveillance, improved molecular diagnostics, and locally calibrated early warning.
papers.journal: Clinical microbiology and infection : the official publication of the European Society of Clinical Microbiology and Infectious Diseases

papers.title: Hantavirus infection in emergency radiology: Imaging manifestations, pathophysiology, and infection control considerations.
papers.abstract: In April 2026, several cases of severe respiratory illnesses were reported aboard the cruise ship MV Hondius during its voyage from Argentina. Subsequent laboratory testing identified Andes virus (ANDV), a hantavirus subtype, with rare but documented human-to-human transmission. Although hantavirus infections are uncommon, both hantavirus pulmonary syndrome (HPS) and hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) are associated with substantial morbidity and mortality. Their rapid progression and potential need for intensive respiratory support continue to pose important challenges for emergency departments, intensive care units, and radiology services. Because pulmonary imaging findings often evolve quickly, radiologists play a critical role in early recognition and triage. This review provides an overview of the pathophysiology, imaging manifestations, and operational considerations relevant to hantavirus infection in emergency radiology practice.

papers.title: EPIZOOTIC AND EPIDEMIC SITUATION OF HANTAVIRUS INFECTION IN THE WORLD
papers.abstract: This review examines the current epidemiological and epizootic situation in natural foci of hantavirus diseases across various regions of the world. Today, hantavirus diseases represent a significant threat to the sanitary and epidemiological well-being of populations worldwide, capable of seriously complicating the epidemiological situation. Approximately 200,000 cases are registered worldwide annually, although the intensity and dynamics of morbidity vary considerably across regions. In China — the country with the highest annual number of cases in the world — the overall incidence trend is declining. Ukraine is a natural endemic focus for the spread of hantaviruses that cause hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS). Given climate change, which stimulates rodent migration and reproduction, epidemiological risks for the rural population and military personnel are increasing. Data on the spread of hantavirus infection in the regions of Southeast Asia and the African continent require further study; however, it is quite evident that hantavirus infection is an underestimated public health problem in these regions, and its true scale — given the wide distribution of reservoir hosts — may be considerably greater than currently known. Keywords: hantavirus diseases, hantavirus pulmonary syndrome, hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome, epidemiological situation, natural reservoirs, pathogens.

analysis.main_directions: It highlights the worldwide health risk of hantavirus disease, the influence of climate‑driven rodent dynamics, and the paucity of data from Southeast Asia and Africa (A2, A6, A7, A8).
analysis.current_state: Approximately 200,000 cases are reported annually with marked regional variation; incidence is declining in China, while Ukraine remains a natural endemic focus for HFRS (A3, A4, A5).
analysis.gaps: Surveillance and epidemiological data are insufficient for many regions, especially Southeast Asia and Africa, leading to likely underestimation of disease burden (A7, A8).

papers.title: Multi-Country Human-to-Human Andes Virus Outbreak on a Cruise Ship: A Disaster Report on Prehospital, Health Care Facility, and Public Health System Challenges - Essential Knowledge for Frontline Clinicians.
papers.abstract: Abstract The Andes Virus (ANDV) outbreak reported on May 2, 2026, aboard a luxury vessel departing from Ushuaia, Patagonia, Argentina, was caused by an Orthohantavirus unique in its person-to-person transmissibility in contrast to zoonotic transmission characteristic of better-known hantaviruses. Containment required coordinated international management because passengers and crew embarked and disembarked at several international ports-of-call prior to outbreak recognition, resulting in cross-border transmission potential. Among those who disembarked, several traveled on flights to various destinations. Cases subsequently manifested in multiple countries, including Tristan da Cunha, Spain, France, Switzerland, South Africa, Canada, and The Netherlands. Upon notification, international health authorities implemented containment measures, such as contact tracing, quarantine, and isolation. Uniquely, ANDV poses distinctive risks due to its immediately prodromal presymptomatic transmission potential, initial non-specific flu-like symptoms, prolonged incubation period, conceivable long-term neurologic and endocrinologic sequalae, high case fatality rates (CFRs), and possibility of international dissemination. This report describes the successful management of a multi-national outbreak associated with cruise-ship travel, a setting with unique challenges. It also examines implications and challenges for prehospital, health care facility, and public health systems for future ANDV outbreaks. The event was characterized by delayed recognition, international spread, and complex coordination across multiple jurisdictions and sectors, including medical and public health authorities, policy- and decision-makers, crisis and emergency risk-communication experts, media, logistics, transportation, and security. Rapid implementation of public health measures coupled with clinician implementation of the Identify-Isolate-Inform (3I) model, a clinical framework to detect and prevent the spread of infectious disease, at the prehospital and health care facility levels are critical actions that can contain future ANDV outbreaks.

By the conclusion of the outbreak, there were a total of 13 cases (12 confirmed and one probable for ANDV). According to data from the vessel’s operator, Oceanwide Expeditions (Vlissingen, The Netherlands), least 33 passengers from 12 nations (Canada, Denmark, Germany, the Netherlands, New Zealand, Saint Kitts and Nevis, Singapore, Sweden, Switzerland, Türkiye, the UK, and the United States) disembarked the MV Hondius at St. Helena, a British island in the South Atlantic, between April 21-24.9 Other scientific publications cite slightly different numbers,10 highlighting the challenges with data collection and effective communication during a rapidly evolving outbreak. On April 25, most of those who left the ship traveled together on the only commercial flight out of St. Helena, landing in Johannesburg, South Africa later that day. From there, most continued onward to other world-wide destinations. United States residents returned to five different states (Arizona, California, Georgia, Texas, and Virginia), each with its own health authority. All these passengers traveled unmonitored while potentially infectious (Figure 1). While data are inconclusive, WHO endorses the working hypothesis that the index patient was infected before boarding the ship in Ushuaia on April 1, likely through zoonotic exposure to ANDV in Patagonia. A New England Journal of Medicine article published on May 20, 2026 reported he developed symptoms on approximately April 3.11 Given the typical incubation period of two to six weeks, this strongly supports the theory that infection was not acquired on the ship. His condition deteriorated rapidly, and he died onboard ten days after departure. His body was removed 13 days later in St. Helena. The second case, the wife of the index case, was a passenger on the flight from St. Helena to O.R. Tambo International Airport in Johannesburg, South Africa. After the UK’s notification to WHO on May 2, the remaining passengers were restricted from leaving the ship and remained in their cabins. Between May 4-5, three symptomatic passengers were medically evacuated from the ship to the Netherlands. On May 6, as part of the organized disaster response, an emergency team boarded the MV Hondius. The team consisted of two public health experts from WHO and the European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control (ECDC; Solna, Sweden) for situation assessment, and two Dutch medical experts for clinical assessment and management. After anchoring at Tenerife, Canary Islands, 85 passengers and 35 crew disembarked for immediate medical evacuation and repa- triation. Asymptomatic Spanish nationals were transported to a military facility in Madrid, Spain, and the others to their countries of origin. The WHO recommended that all remain in prolonged quarantine (42 days). The WHO asked countries with repatriated nationals to initiate precautionary contact tracing. Persons were categorized as high risk (placed in quarantine) or low risk (performed active self- monitoring) continuing for 42 days following last known exposure.12 Source The investigators obtained clinical and treatment data exclusively from publicly available sources, such as peer-reviewed literature and aggregate event descriptions. Observations Epidemiological Characteristics of Orthohantavirus In humans, pathogenic rodent-borne orthohantaviruses cause two major severe syndromes depending broadly on viral phylogeog- raphy: (1) hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS), caused mainly by Eurasian species and characterized by capillary leak and acute kidney injury (AKI); and (2) HCPS, caused by American species and characterized by rapidly progressive noncardiogenic pulmonary edema, respiratory failure, and often, cardiogenic shock (Table 2 and Figure 2).7,13 The primary reservoir for ANDV is the long-tailed pygmy rice rat (Oligoryzomys longicaudatus).14 Spillovers to humans result from inhalation of aerosolized dried viral particles from con- taminated rodent urine, feces, or saliva.15 Andes Virus has a reproductive number (R0) of 2.12 – meaning, prior to outbreak containment measures, each infected person, on average, spreads the virus to more than two susceptible others, and so on, which can lead to an exponential rise in the epidemiologic curve.5 Effective public health measures can reduce the R0 to below 1.00, thereby halting the outbreak and preventing a global pandemic. papers.title: Of mice and men: Updates on hantavirus disease and diagnostics.
papers.abstract: Hantaviruses are a diverse and widespread group of zoonotic viruses under the Orthohantavirus genus that can cause severe acute cardiopulmonary or renal disease. Hantavirus species are grouped generally as either New World or Old World based on geographic distribution, which is influenced by their respective host reservoir including rodents. Although there is no specific treatment for hantaviruses, recognizing clinical presentation and interpreting laboratory results for case identification can improve patient management. Here we review the epidemiology, clinical manifestations, and diagnostic testing options for hantavirus infection.
papers.journal: Journal of clinical virology : the official publication of the Pan American Society for Clinical Virology

Future research: Develop specific antivirals, validate rapid diagnostics, and enhance reservoir surveillance.

papers.title: Andes Virus - A Clinical Review.
papers.abstract: Andes virus (ANDV) is the sole orthohantavirus with documented human-to-human transmission. We summarize the epidemiology and clinical features of ANDV infection and review best practices in clinical management, as based on published expert consensus guidelines, field experience, and clinical trials. We also evaluate currently available and investigational treatments (including the use of antiviral agents), assess emerging monoclonal antibody therapies, and outline prospects for vaccine development. Finally, we discuss important infection prevention and control measures.
papers.journal: The New England journal of medicine

papers.title: Hantavirus Infection Beyond the Lung: A Multi-Organ Radiological Perspective on Diagnosis, Imaging Modalities, and Precautionary Measures for Radiology Departments.
papers.abstract: Hantavirus infection is an emerging zoonotic disease with worldwide relevance, associated with significant morbidity and mortality through hantavirus pulmonary syndrome and hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome. After recent reports, including a cluster of severe cases reported to the World Health Organization in 2026, increasing attention has been directed toward its clinical, pathological, and radiological spectrum. Radiology departments, as one of the most important health care providers involved in imaging for disease confirmation, detection of complications, and assessment of involvement of different body organs, should be familiar with the manifestations of suspected patients, the most appropriate imaging requests, and the precautionary measures required within the department to prevent disease transmission to both health care personnel and other patients undergoing imaging procedures. Therefore, in this review, we aimed to present recent clinical and radiological findings, as well as precautionary interventions that should be implemented in radiology departments.
papers.journal: Journal of the American College of Radiology : JACR

analysis.background: Hantavirus infection is an emerging zoonotic disease with global relevance, causing severe pulmonary and renal syndromes (A1). Recent WHO-reported clusters in 2026 have heightened focus on its clinical and radiological spectrum (A2).
analysis.main_directions: The review emphasizes radiology departments' role in confirming diagnosis, detecting complications, and evaluating multi‑organ involvement, and outlines appropriate imaging requests and safety measures (A3).
analysis.current_state: Radiology services are recognized as pivotal for hantavirus assessment, yet familiarity with the full spectrum of organ manifestations and optimal imaging protocols varies (A3).
analysis.gaps: Evidence on standardized multi‑organ imaging criteria and comprehensive infection‑control practices in radiology settings remains limited (A4).
analysis.future_research: Further studies should define optimal imaging modalities for extra‑pulmonary disease, validate precautionary protocols, and assess their impact on transmission risk in radiology departments (A4).

analysis.summary_en: Background: Hantavirus is a global zoonosis causing severe lung and kidney disease, with recent WHO clusters prompting renewed attention (A1, A2). Main directions: Radiology departments are central to diagnosis, organ involvement assessment, and infection control (A3). Current state: Radiology is key for hantavirus evaluation, but consistent knowledge of multi‑organ imaging and safety practices is uneven (A3). Gaps: Standardized imaging criteria and comprehensive departmental precautions are under‑studied (A4). Future research: Define optimal imaging for extra‑pulmonary disease, validate safety protocols, and measure their effectiveness in radiology settings (A4).

papers.title: Beyond the Kidney and Lung: Cutaneous and Mucosal Clues to Human Hantavirus Disease.
papers.abstract: Hantaviruses are rodent-borne viruses that cause two overlapping vascular syndromes in humans: hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome, including nephropathia epidemica, and hantavirus pulmonary/cardiopulmonary syndrome. Although dermatologists are rarely central to hantavirus care, early visible abnormalities may occur on the skin, mucosa, and ocular surface. This narrative review synthesizes the dermatologic and mucocutaneous manifestations of human hantavirus disease, with emphasis on signs that should prompt diagnostic suspicion in dermatology, emergency, travel-medicine, and infectious-disease settings. The dermatologic signal is strongest in hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome, where facial or upper-torso flushing, conjunctival and pharyngeal injection, petechiae, purpura, ecchymoses, and mucosal bleeding may appear during the febrile or hemorrhagic phases. These findings are not pathognomonic, but their diagnostic value increases when they occur with rodent or outbreak exposure, thrombocytopenia or coagulopathy, and renal abnormalities such as proteinuria, hematuria, or acute kidney injury. In hantavirus pulmonary/cardiopulmonary syndrome, particularly infections caused by New World hantaviruses, visible cutaneous involvement is less prominent and may be absent despite severe pulmonary endothelial disease. We propose a practical dermatology-oriented trigger for suspicion based on exposure history, abrupt febrile illness, nephro-pulmonary involvement, thrombocytopenia, and vascular mucocutaneous findings. Hantavirus should be considered when otherwise unexplained vascular skin or mucosal signs occur in a febrile patient with thrombocytopenia, renal involvement, hypoxemia, or compatible exposure. The skin rarely diagnoses hantavirus alone, but it may shorten time to testing, supportive care, and public-health notification.

analysis.background: Hantaviruses are rodent‑borne viruses that cause hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) and hantavirus pulmonary/cardiopulmonary syndrome (HPS), yet cutaneous and mucosal signs are rarely emphasized.
analysis.main_directions: The review surveys dermatologic and mucosal manifestations—facial flushing, petechiae, purpura, and mucosal bleeding in HFRS and their relative absence in New World HPS—to inform dermatology, emergency, travel‑medicine, and infectious‑disease practice.
analysis.current_state: Skin and mucosal findings are most prominent during the febrile/hemorrhagic phase of HFRS, but they are nonspecific and often absent in HPS.
analysis.gaps: These cutaneous signs are not pathognomonic and existing data are limited, reducing confidence in dermatologic diagnosis of hantavirus infection.
analysis.future_research: Prospective validation of the proposed dermatology‑oriented suspicion trigger and studies measuring the impact of early skin findings on testing and outcomes are warranted.

analysis.summary_en: Background: Hantaviruses cause HFRS and HPS, but skin signs are under‑recognized (A1). Main directions: The review details flushing, petechiae, purpura, and mucosal bleeding in HFRS and their rarity in New World HPS to guide clinicians (A2, A4, A6). Current state: Cutaneous findings peak in HFRS febrile/hemorrhagic phases yet are nonspecific and often missing in HPS (A4, A6). Gaps: Lack of pathognomonic signs and limited systematic data hinder reliable dermatologic diagnosis (A5). Future research: Validate the dermatology‑oriented suspicion trigger and assess early skin signs’ diagnostic value (A7).

papers.title_zh: 超越肾脏和肺部:人类汉坦病毒疾病的皮肤和黏膜线索。

analysis_zh.background: 汉坦病毒es 是啮齿动物传播的病毒,可导致 肾综合征出血热(HFRS)和 汉坦病毒 肺/心肺综合征(HPS),但皮肤和黏膜体征很少被强调。
analysis_zh.main_directions: 本综述调查了皮肤和黏膜表现——面部潮红、瘀点、紫癜以及 HFRS 中的黏膜出血,并在新世界 HPS 中相对缺乏——以为皮肤科、急诊、旅行医学和传染病实践提供信息。
analysis_zh.current_state: 皮肤和黏膜发现最突出于 HFRS 的发热/出血期,但它们非特异性,且在 HPS 中常常缺失。
analysis_zh.gaps: 这些皮肤体征并非特征性,且现有数据有限,降低了对 汉坦病毒 感染的皮肤学诊断信心。
analysis_zh.future_research: 需要前瞻性验证所提出的面向皮肤科的疑虑触发器,并开展研究评估早期皮肤发现对检测和结局的影响。

papers.title: Hantavirus in Dentistry: Occupational Exposure Considerations and a Proposed Tiered Infection Prevention and Control Framework-A Narrative Review.
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT Objective The aim of this study is to synthesize evidence on hantavirus transmission and occupational exposure pathways relevant to dentistry, and to propose an evidence‐informed tiered infection prevention and control (IPC) framework that distinguishes established from theoretical risk. Material and Methods The initial narrative search covered database inception through May 15, 2026 in MEDLINE/PubMed, Embase, Web of Science, Scopus, Google Scholar, and WHO/CDC/ECDC/OSHA sources, followed by a targeted PubMed/MEDLINE and public‐health guidance update through August 18, 2026. Approximately 1450 records were identified. After duplicate removal, 1070 records were subjected to title/abstract screening, 215 full‐text records were assessed for eligibility, and 45 sources were included in the final synthesis, comprising 34 peer‐reviewed publications and 11 gray‐literature or public‐health guidance sources. Results Environmental exposure to infected‐rodent contamination is the established occupational pathway. Limited person‐to‐person transmission is documented for the Andes virus (ANDV), but no dental transmission has been reported. ANDV RNA and culture‐based infectivity have been demonstrated in some oral/respiratory fluids; however, dental‐aerosol transmission has not been shown. Dental‐specific occupational risk therefore remains unquantified. Conclusions No dental transmission has been documented, and patient‐related risk remains uncertain. Standard precautions and rodent control are foundational; suspected or confirmed ANDV warrants transmission‐based precautions and airborne precautions for aerosol‐generating procedures according to current guidance. The proposed dental tiers are evidence‐informed, author‐derived, and unvalidated.

Standard precautions and rodent control are foundational; suspected or confirmed ANDV warrants transmission‐based precautions and airborne precautions for aerosol‐generating procedures according to current guidance. The proposed dental tiers are evidence‐informed, author‐derived, and unvalidated.

analysis.background: The review aims to synthesize evidence on hantavirus transmission pathways relevant to dentistry and to propose a tiered infection‑prevention framework (A1).
analysis.main_directions: It examines environmental rodent exposure, limited person‑to‑person transmission of Andes virus (ANDV), detection of ANDV RNA in oral/respiratory fluids, the absence of documented dental transmission, and an author‑derived IPC tier system (A5; A6; A7; A8; A13).
analysis.current_state: Environmental rodent contact is the established occupational route, ANDV can be present in oral fluids but aerosol transmission in dental settings has not been demonstrated, and no dental cases have been reported (A5; A6; A8; A10).
analysis.gaps: The quantitative risk for dental personnel remains unquantified, the proposed tiered framework is unvalidated, and data on aerosol‑mediated transmission in dental procedures are lacking (A9; A13).
analysis.future_research: Epidemiological studies to measure dental exposure risk, validation of the tiered IPC model, experimental work on aerosol infectivity of hantavirus, and surveillance of hantavirus in dental clinics are needed (A9; A13).

analysis.summary_en: Background: The review synthesizes hantavirus transmission evidence for dentistry and proposes a tiered IPC framework (A1). Main directions: It covers rodent exposure, limited ANDV person‑to‑person spread, oral fluid infectivity, lack of dental cases, and an author‑derived tier system (A5; A6; A7; A8; A13). Current state: Rodent exposure is the established risk; ANDV RNA appears in oral fluids but dental aerosol transmission is unproven and no cases reported (A5; A6; A8; A10). Gaps: Dental occupational risk is unquantified, the tiered framework is unvalidated, and aerosol transmission data are scarce (A9; A13). Future research: Conduct exposure quantification studies, validate IPC tiers, test aerosol infectivity, and implement surveillance in dental settings (A9; A13).

papers.title: Characteristics and Superspreading Potential of Andes Virus Person-to-Person Transmission.
papers.abstract: By using historical contact tracing data, we estimated that 23.4% of case-patients caused 80% of Andes virus (ANDV) person-to-person transmission. We demonstrated a low but nonnegligible probability of observing a large-scale ANDV infection outbreak in a rodent-free setting consisting of close contacts, despite the historically self-limited person-to-person transmission of ANDV.

source_records.title: Characteristics and Superspreading Potential of Andes Virus Person-to-Person Transmission.
source_records.abstract: By using historical contact tracing data, we estimated that 23.4% of case-patients caused 80% of Andes virus (ANDV) person-to-person transmission. We demonstrated a low but nonnegligible probability of observing a large-scale ANDV infection outbreak in a rodent-free setting consisting of close contacts, despite the historically self-limited person-to-person transmission of ANDV.

analysis.background: not reported in the supplied evidence
analysis.methods: The study used historical contact tracing data to assess Andes virus (ANDV) person‑to‑person transmission; specific location, host population, and detailed analytical methods were not reported.
analysis.results: 23.4% of case‑patients were responsible for 80% of ANDV person‑to‑person transmission, indicating superspreading; the authors also demonstrated a low but nonnegligible probability of a large‑scale outbreak among close contacts in a rodent‑free setting.
analysis.contribution: The work quantifies the superspreading potential of ANDV and highlights the risk of sizable outbreaks even without rodent reservoirs, informing surveillance and public‑health preparedness.
analysis.limitations: Only the abstract is available, limiting detail on methods, sample size, and quantitative estimates; no full‑text data were provided.

analysis.summary_en: Background: not reported in the supplied evidence. Methods: Historical contact tracing data were analyzed; location and detailed methods not reported. Results: 23.4% of case‑patients caused 80% of ANDV transmission, and a low but nonnegligible chance of a large outbreak among close contacts in a rodent‑free setting was demonstrated. Contribution: Provides quantitative insight into ANDV superspreading and outbreak risk, aiding surveillance and public‑health planning. Limitations: Only abstract data are available, restricting methodological and quantitative detail.
